summary: Explains how the ISSN, the number used to identify serials such as magazines and journals, can be used within the URN framework as its own namespace. This document is historic and was replaced by RFC 8254.

eli5.summary: Magazines already have an ID number. This shows how to turn that number into a permanent Internet-style name. This note is old and was replaced.

questions: how to use issn as a urn
what is the issn check digit
subtitle: How the number printed on magazines and journals can double as a permanent Uniform Resource Name.

tldr.problem: Libraries already identify serials such as journals and newspapers with the ISSN, but the URN framework needed a registered namespace before that number could be used as a name on the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC shows that an ISSN meets the URN requirements, describes a central resolver run by the ISSN International Centre that maps an ISSN to one or several URLs, and includes the namespace registration form for the NID ISSN.
tldr.outcome: This memo is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 8254, so it records an early demonstrator rather than a current specification.

today: RFC 3044 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 8254, which is the document to read for the ISSN namespace today. This memo remains a record of the early ISSN-IC demonstrator described in its own text.

sections.title: Why Use the ISSN as a URN
sections.content:
The ISSN International Centre ran a URN implementation in 1999 and 2000. It builds on the functional compatibility between the ISSN and the URN, and it shows that URNs can absorb identifiers from well established schemes used by the bibliographic community.

The RFC says plainly that this is a demonstrator. To go further, a responsible body or infrastructure is needed to assign namespaces and manage an RDS/NAPTR global resolution framework. The document also contains a namespace registration form, so some paragraphs appear twice.
sections.eli5: A library already numbers every magazine. This note tests whether those numbers can also work as permanent names online.

sections.title: The ISSN System
sections.content:
The ISSN (International Standard Serial Number) is defined in ISO 3297:1998. Each ISSN is a unique identifier for one serial publication, whatever the medium. Serials include periodicals, newspapers, annuals and the journals, series and proceedings of societies.

An ISSN is eight digits. The last one is a check digit, calculated modulus 11 with weights 8 to 2, and it can be X where the value would be 10. The number carries no meaning about language, country or publisher. It is shown as two groups of four digits joined by a hyphen, for example ISSN 1560-1560.

Each ISSN is tied to a key title, a form of the title built to be unique in the ISSN Register. The register is kept by the ISSN International Centre and is fed by National Centres, which identify serials published in their own countries.
sections.eli5: An ISSN is like a serial number stamped on a magazine, with a final check character that helps catch typing mistakes.

sections.title: Meeting the URN Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the requirements of RFC 1737 and says the ISSN satisfies each one. It is global in scope and never assigned to two resources. Once assigned, an ISSN is never re-assigned. The register also covers ceased serials, which supports persistence. The ISSN is already a legacy naming system, and the ISSN International Centre built a resolver for translation to URLs.

On syntax, an ISSN namespace uses no reserved characters, so percent-encoding is never required. An example is urn:ISSN:1046-8188. Two extra comparison rules apply: hyphens are dropped before comparing, and a lowercase x is normalised to uppercase.
sections.eli5: The note checks the ISSN against a list of rules for good permanent names and says it passes every one.

sections.title: Resolving an ISSN URN
sections.content:
The demonstrator translates an ISSN URN into electronic locations: the bibliographic description and, if it exists online, the serial itself. Because those URLs are not persistent, they must be checked regularly and corrected in the resolver database.

Four pieces of work are described. A centralised resolver on one server at the ISSN International Centre maps an ISSN to one or several URLs. A robot called the URL Watcher checks the stored URLs and records broken or redirected ones. A browser plug-in for Netscape Communicator and MS-Explorer lets a user type a name such as urn:ISSN:1560-1560 into the address box. Clicking an ISSN on an HTML page gives the same result.

For global resolution, RFC 2611 says a namespace must be registered in a Resolution Discovery System such as NAPTR. The authors state that their system is flexible enough to fit an RDS/NAPTR framework.
sections.eli5: A lookup desk turns the magazine number into web addresses, and a robot keeps checking that those addresses still work.

sections.title: The Namespace Registration
sections.content:
Section 5 is the registration form for the Namespace ID ISSN, version 1, dated 2000-08-28. The syntax is NNNN-NNNC, where N is a digit and C is a digit or X. Examples given are urn:ISSN:0259-000X and urn:ISSN:1560-1560.

Uniqueness comes from the ISSN definition, and a different ISSN is assigned to each medium. Persistence comes from the ISSN Register. For lexical equivalence, an x check character is made uppercase and the hyphen may be omitted. The first resolution step is the centralised demonstrator, and the second is expected to be global resolution through RDS/NAPTR.
sections.eli5: This part is the official form that says, here is the name of our naming club and here are its rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The namespace defines no additional reserved characters, so the RFC says it adds no security considerations. No validation mechanism is specified today, and the scope is global.
sections.eli5: Nothing new here needs guarding, because the names use only ordinary characters.

fields.name: NNN
fields.desc: Three more digits, 0 to 9, after the hyphen.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Check character: a digit or X, modulus 11 with weights 8 to 2.
